front: What is an upper bound of a set A of real numbers?
back: A real number u with a ≤ u for every a in A. A set with an upper bound is bounded above (Section 1).

front: What is the supremum of A?
back: An upper bound s of A with s ≤ u for every upper bound u of A, that is, a least upper bound. Two suprema of one set are equal (Section 1).

front: State the completeness of the real numbers (Definition 1.1).
back: Every nonempty subset of R that is bounded above has a supremum in R. It is the defining property of R, taken without proof.

front: Theorem 1.2 (Archimedean property). Hypotheses: x is a real number; every nonempty subset of R bounded above has a supremum; N is the set of natural numbers, and n in N implies n + 1 in N. What is the conclusion?
back: There is n in N with n > x.

front: Theorem 1.3 (nested intervals). Hypotheses: for each n in N, a_n ≤ b_n are real and I_n = [a_n, b_n]; I_{n+1} ⊆ I_n for every n; every nonempty subset of R bounded above has a supremum. What is the conclusion?
back: There is a real s with s in I_n for every n.

front: Corollary 1.4 (a single point). Hypotheses: for each n in N, a_n ≤ b_n are real and I_n = [a_n, b_n]; I_{n+1} ⊆ I_n for every n; every nonempty subset of R bounded above has a supremum; and the lengths b_n − a_n tend to 0. What does the intersection of the I_n contain?
back: Exactly one real number.

front: Lemma 1.5. For S = {x ≥ 0 : x² < 2} and a real m ≥ 0, what does the two-case test say?
back: Either m is in S, when m² < 2, or m is an upper bound of S, when m² ≥ 2. In particular 2 is an upper bound of S.

front: Theorem 1.6 (bisection brackets the supremum). Hypotheses: S0 is a nonempty subset of R bounded above; a_0 is in S0, b_0 is an upper bound of S0, and a_0 ≤ b_0; for every m with a_0 ≤ m ≤ b_0, either m is in S0 or m is an upper bound of S0. What does bisection give?
back: For every n, a_n ≤ sup S0 ≤ b_n, and b_n − a_n = (b_0 − a_0)/2^n. The midpoint replaces a_n when it lies in S0, and replaces b_n otherwise.

front: Proposition 1.7. Hypotheses: S = {x ≥ 0 : x² < 2}, and s = sup S, which exists because 0 is in S and 2 is an upper bound (Lemma 1.5). What is s²?
back: s² = 2. Both s² < 2 and s² > 2 are impossible.

front: In Lab 1, what bracket does bisection give after 12 steps from [0, 2], and what is its width?
back: [181/128, 2897/2048], with width 1/2048. The brackets are exact fractions.

front: In Lab 1, which step is the first whose bracket width is below 1/1000?
back: Step 11, where the width is 1/1024.
basis: Lab 1 (exact width comparison; Problem E2 gives the same step from 2^(1−n))

front: In Lab 1, how many of the 13 brackets satisfy a² < 2 ≤ b²?
back: All 13.
basis: Lab 1 (exact check over the finite run)

front: Does the set of rational x ≥ 0 with x² < 2 have a least upper bound among the rational numbers?
back: No. A rational least upper bound q would satisfy q² = 2, and no rational number does (M1, Lesson 2, Corollary 2.6).
basis: Section 4 (canon break 1), from Proposition 1.7 and M1, Lesson 2, Corollary 2.6

front: Does a bounded set always have a largest element?
back: No. S = {x ≥ 0 : x² < 2} is bounded above by 2, but its supremum s satisfies s² = 2, so s is not in S and S has no largest element (Misconception 1).

front: Why does Theorem 1.6 apply to S = {x ≥ 0 : x² < 2}, even though the rational set S_rat has no least upper bound among the rationals?
back: S is a nonempty subset of R bounded above by 2 (Lemma 1.5), so Definition 1.1 supplies its supremum in R. Completeness is a property of R, not of the rational numbers (Misconception 2).

front: Does bisection with enough steps land exactly on the supremum?
back: No. Every bracket endpoint is rational, and a rational supremum would have square 2, which is impossible (Misconception 3).

front: When does a sequence (s_n) of real numbers converge to L (Definition 1.1)?
back: When for every ε > 0 there is N in N with |s_n − L| < ε for every n ≥ N.

front: Proposition 1.2 (uniqueness of the limit). Hypotheses: s_n → L and s_n → L' for real numbers L and L'. What is the conclusion?
back: L = L'. So the notation lim s_n is meaningful when the limit exists.

front: What is a Cauchy sequence (Definition 2.1)?
back: A sequence for which every ε > 0 has an N with |s_m − s_n| < ε for all m, n ≥ N. The N depends on ε, and no limit appears in the definition.

front: Proposition 2.2 (convergent implies Cauchy). Hypothesis: s_n → L for some real L. What is the conclusion?
back: The sequence (s_n) is Cauchy.

front: Lemma 2.3. Hypothesis: (s_n) is a Cauchy sequence of real numbers. What is the conclusion?
back: There is a real C with |s_n| ≤ C for every n. A Cauchy sequence is bounded.

front: Lemma 2.4 (greatest lower bound). Hypotheses: B is a nonempty set of reals bounded below; every nonempty subset of R bounded above has a supremum. What is the conclusion?
back: B has a greatest lower bound L, and for every η > 0 some b in B satisfies b < L + η.

front: Theorem 2.5 (Cauchy criterion for real sequences). Hypotheses: (s_n) is a Cauchy sequence of real numbers; every nonempty subset of R bounded above has a supremum. What is the conclusion?
back: (s_n) converges to some L in R.

front: What does it mean for the series Σ a_n to converge (Definition 3.1)?
back: The partial sums S_N, each the sum of a_k for k from 1 to N, converge, and the sum of the series is their limit.

front: Corollary 3.2 (Cauchy criterion for series). Hypotheses: (a_n) is a sequence of real numbers with partial sums S_N; every nonempty subset of R bounded above has a supremum. What is the conclusion?
back: Σ a_n converges if and only if for every ε > 0 there is N with |the sum of a_k for k from n+1 to m| < ε for all m > n ≥ N.

front: Proposition 3.3 (harmonic partial sums are not Cauchy). Hypothesis: H_n = the sum of 1/k for k from 1 to n, for integers n ≥ 1. What is the conclusion?
back: H_{2N} − H_N ≥ 1/2 for every integer N ≥ 1, so the harmonic series diverges.

front: Lemma 3.4 (a geometric tail). Hypotheses: G_N = the sum of 1/2^k for k from 1 to N, with G_0 = 0; n and m are integers with 0 ≤ n < m. What is G_m − G_n?
Proposition 3.5. Hypotheses: G_N as in Lemma 3.4, ε = 1/2^10, and N an integer with N ≥ 0. What is the conclusion?
back: |G_m − G_n| < ε for all m > n ≥ N if and only if N ≥ 10.

front: If the terms of a series tend to zero, does the series converge?
back: No. The terms 1/n tend to zero, but the harmonic series diverges (Proposition 3.3). Tending to zero is necessary for convergence and not sufficient.

front: If consecutive terms get closer together, is the sequence Cauchy?
back: Not necessarily. For s_n = √n the gaps tend to zero, but the sequence is unbounded, and a Cauchy sequence is bounded (Lemma 2.3).

front: Does a Cauchy sequence of rational numbers have a rational limit?
back: Not necessarily. The left bisection endpoints of Lesson 1 form a Cauchy sequence of rationals whose limit sup S is not rational (Section 4).

front: In Lab 1, how many of the 200 pairs (N, 2N) have gap S_2N − S_N at least 1/2?
back: All 200 of 200 pairs.
basis: Lab 1 (finite range N = 1 to 200; Proposition 3.3 covers all N)

front: In Lab 1, from which index N does the geometric Cauchy test with ε = 1/1024 pass in the printed search?
back: N = 10. The test fails for N from 0 to 9.
basis: Lab 1 (search over m ≤ 60; Proposition 3.5 covers all m)

front: In Lab 1, how many pairs with 0 ≤ n < m ≤ 60 satisfy the identity of Lemma 3.4?
back: All 1830 pairs.
basis: Lab 1 (exact check on a finite range; Lemma 3.4 proves the identity)

front: What does it mean for f: D → R to be continuous at x0 in ε–δ form (Definition 1.1)?
back: For every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that each x in D with |x − x0| < δ satisfies |f(x) − f(x0)| < ε. The function is continuous on D when it is continuous at every point of D.

front: What is uniform continuity of f on D (Section 3)?
back: For every ε > 0 there is one δ > 0 with |f(x) − f(y)| < ε whenever x and y are in D and |x − y| < δ. One δ serves all points at once.

front: Lemma 1.3. Hypothesis: x is real with |x − 2| ≤ 1. What is the conclusion?
Proposition 1.4. Hypothesis: D = R, f(x) = x², and x0 = 2. What is the conclusion?
back: f is continuous at 2, and δ = min{1, ε/5} works for each ε > 0.

front: Proposition 1.5. Hypotheses: f and g map D to R, x0 is in D, and both are continuous at x0. What is the conclusion?
back: f + g is continuous at x0.

front: Proposition 2.1 (sequential characterization). Hypotheses: D is a subset of R, f: D → R, and x0 is in D. What is the conclusion?
back: f is continuous at x0 if and only if f(x_n) → f(x0) for every sequence x_n in D with x_n → x0.

front: Proposition 2.2. Hypothesis: f(x) = x² on R and x_n → 2. What is the conclusion?
back: x_n² → 4.

front: Proposition 3.1. Hypothesis: f(x) = x² on R, with ε = 1. What is the conclusion?
back: For every δ > 0 there are x, y in R with |x − y| < δ and |f(x) − f(y)| ≥ 1. So x² is not uniformly continuous on R.

front: What is the least constant c with |x² − 4| ≤ c|x − 2| for every real x with |x − 2| ≤ 1?
back: c = 5. Lemma 1.3 gives the bound with 5, and at x = 3 the left side equals 5 while |x − 2| = 1, so no smaller c works (Problem R1).

front: Does one δ serve every ε and every point?
back: No. δ depends on ε and on x0. The choice δ = min{1, ε/5} at the point 2 fails at the point 10 when ε = 1: with δ = 1/5, the point 10.1 lies within δ of 10, and |10.1² − 100| = 2.01 ≥ 1 (Misconception 1).

front: Is a function that is defined at x0 continuous there?
back: No. f(x) = x for x ≠ 1 and f(1) = 5 is defined at 1 but is not continuous there, because values near 1 are near 1, not near 5 (canon break 2).

front: Does one sequence converging to x0 with f(x_n) → f(x0) show continuity?
back: No. Proposition 2.1 needs every such sequence. For f = 0 at 0 and at each 1/k, and f = 1 elsewhere, the sequence x_n = 1/n gives f(x_n) = 0, but y_n = 2/(2n + 1) gives f(y_n) = 1 for every n (Misconception 3).

front: In Lab 1, how many grid points lie within δ = 1/50 of 2?
back: Seven points, namely k from −3 to 3.

front: In Lab 1 with δ = 1/10, how many grid points have |x − 2| < 1/10 and |x² − 4| ≥ 1/10?
back: 29 points.
basis: Lab 1 (exact grid; Problem E3 counts 15 and 14 on the two sides of 2)

front: Does the bound |x² − 4| ≤ 5|x − 2| hold at all 401 grid points in Lab 1?
back: Yes, at all 401 points. The grid is a finite check. Lemma 1.3 gives the bound for every x with |x − 2| ≤ 1.
basis: Lab 1 (exact grid); Lemma 1.3 is the proof

front: What are the three axioms of a metric on X (Definition 1.1)?
back: (M1) d(x, y) ≥ 0, with d(x, y) = 0 only when x = y; (M2) d(x, y) = d(y, x); (M3) d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all x, y, z.

front: What are the open ball B(x, r) and an open set in a metric space (Section 2)?
back: B(x, r) = {y : d(x, y) < r}. A set U is open when every x in U has some r > 0 with B(x, r) inside U.

front: When does a sequence (x_n) in a metric space converge to x (Definition 3.1)?
back: When d(x_n, x) → 0: for every ε > 0 there is N with d(x_n, x) < ε for all n ≥ N.

front: What is a Cauchy sequence in a metric space (Definition 3.2)?
back: A sequence for which every ε > 0 has an N with d(x_m, x_n) < ε for all m, n ≥ N.

front: When is a map f: X → Y between metric spaces continuous at x (Definition 4.1)?
back: For every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with d_Y(f(x), f(z)) < ε whenever d_X(x, z) < δ.

front: Proposition 1.4. Hypotheses: x, y, z are points of R², and d2 is the Euclidean distance |x − y|. What is the conclusion?
back: (R², d2) is a metric space. The triangle inequality follows from the Lagrange identity in two dimensions.

front: Proposition 1.7. Hypotheses: S is a nonempty set; f, g, h are bounded real functions on S; d∞(f, g) = sup over x in S of |f(x) − g(x)|; every nonempty subset of R bounded above has a supremum. What is the conclusion?
back: (ℓ∞(S), d∞) is a metric space, and every value d∞(f, g) is a real number.

front: Proposition 2.1. Hypotheses: (X, d) is a metric space; x is in X and r > 0. What is the conclusion?
back: The open ball B(x, r) is an open set.

front: Proposition 3.3. Hypotheses: (X, d) is a metric space; (x_n) converges to x in X. What is the conclusion?
back: (x_n) is a Cauchy sequence.

front: Proposition 3.4 (the plane is complete). Hypotheses: (x^(n)) is a Cauchy sequence in (R², d2); every Cauchy sequence of reals converges to a real number. What is the conclusion?
back: The sequence converges in R², so (R², d2) is complete.

front: Proposition 4.2 (continuity by sequences). Hypotheses: (X, d_X) and (Y, d_Y) are metric spaces, f: X → Y, and x is in X. What is the conclusion?
back: f is continuous at x if and only if d_Y(f(x_n), f(x)) → 0 for every sequence x_n in X with d_X(x_n, x) → 0.

front: Is (0, 1] with the Euclidean distance complete?
back: No. The sequence 1/n is Cauchy in (0, 1] and converges to 0 in R, but 0 is not in (0, 1] (Example 3.6).

front: Is q(x, y) = (x − y)² a metric on R?
back: No. M1 and M2 hold, but M3 fails at the triple (0, 1, 2), since q(0, 2) = 4 exceeds q(0, 1) + q(1, 2) = 2.
basis: Section 5 (canon break 1) and Lab 1 Part C; Empirical 2 lists the two failing triples

front: Is every symmetric function that vanishes only on the diagonal a distance?
back: No. The triangle inequality (M3) is an extra requirement that M1 and M2 do not imply (Misconception 1).

front: Does every Cauchy sequence converge?
back: Only in a complete space. In (0, 1] the Cauchy sequence 1/n has no limit in the space (Misconception 2).

front: Is a set open exactly when it is not closed?
back: No. The set (0, 1] in R is neither open nor closed. It is not open (Remark 2.2), and it is not closed, because every ball about 0 contains points of (0, 1] (Misconception 3).

front: In Lab 1 Part A, how many ordered triples does the Euclidean sample cover?
back: 15625 triples, from the 25 grid points.
basis: Lab 1 Part A (finite sample; Proposition 1.4 covers all points)

front: In Lab 1 Part C, what do the printed values d(0, 2) and d(0, 1) + d(1, 2) show?
back: d(0, 2) = 4 and d(0, 1) + d(1, 2) = 2, so the triangle inequality fails at two triples.
basis: Lab 1 Part C (exact values on three points)

front: In Lab 1 Part B, how many vectors and triples does the sup-distance sample cover?
back: 27 vectors and 19683 triples, with no failures.

front: What is pointwise convergence of f_n to f on S (Definition 1.1)?
back: For each x in S, f_n(x) → f(x). The threshold N may depend on x and ε.

front: What is uniform convergence of f_n to f on S (Definition 1.2)?
back: For each ε > 0 there is one N, not depending on x, with |f_n(x) − f(x)| < ε for all x in S and all n ≥ N. The threshold N is chosen before x.

front: Proposition 1.3(a). Hypotheses: S is nonempty; f_n and f are bounded real functions on S, and d∞(f_n, f) = sup over S of |f_n − f|. What is the conclusion?
back: f_n converges uniformly to f on S if and only if d∞(f_n, f) → 0.

front: Proposition 1.3(b). Hypotheses: S is nonempty; f_n and f are bounded real functions on S. What is the conclusion?
back: Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence.

front: Proposition 2.1 (uniform limits preserve continuity). Hypotheses: (X, d) is a metric space; each f_n: X → R is continuous; f_n converges uniformly to f on X. What is the conclusion?
back: f is continuous at every point of X.

front: Is the pointwise limit of the continuous functions x^n on [0, 1] continuous?
back: No. The limit is 0 on [0, 1) and 1 at 1, and x_k = 1 − 1/k gives f(x_k) = 0 while f(1) = 1 (Example 2.3).

front: Proposition 2.4. Hypotheses: f_n(x) = x^n on [0, 1]; f is the pointwise limit of Example 1.4. What is the conclusion?
back: d∞(f_n, f) = 1 for every n ≥ 1, so the convergence is not uniform on [0, 1].

front: Proposition 2.5. Hypotheses: f_n(x) = x^n with 0 < a < 1, and S = [0, a]. What is the conclusion?
back: d∞(f_n, 0) = a^n for every n ≥ 1, and a^n → 0, so f_n → 0 uniformly on [0, a].

front: Proposition 3.1. Hypotheses: S is nonempty; B(S) is the set of bounded real functions on S with d∞; (f_n) is Cauchy in B(S); every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges (L02, Theorem 2.5). What is the conclusion?
back: There is f in B(S) with d∞(f_n, f) → 0.

front: Proposition 3.2. Hypotheses: (X, d) is a metric space; C_b(X) is the set of bounded continuous real functions on X with d∞; (f_n) is Cauchy in C_b(X). What is the conclusion?
back: There is f in C_b(X) with d∞(f_n, f) → 0.

front: Proposition 2.1 needs one hypothesis beyond continuity of each f_n. Which one, and what does pointwise convergence fail to supply?
back: Uniform convergence of f_n to f on X. Pointwise convergence gives only a threshold N that may depend on x, so it does not preserve continuity (Misconception 1).

front: Does uniform convergence on [0, a] for every a < 1 give uniform convergence on [0, 1]?
back: No. On each [0, a] the sup distance to the limit is a^n, which tends to 0. On [0, 1] it stays at 1 for every n (Propositions 2.4 and 2.5; Misconception 2).

front: If each x has its own threshold N_x, is the convergence uniform?
back: No. Thresholds that depend on x give pointwise convergence. Uniform convergence needs one N that serves all x at once (Misconception 3).

front: In Lab 1 Part A, what sup distance from x^n to 0 on the grid k/100 of [0, 1] is printed for each order?
back: 1, for orders 1, 2, 5, 10 and 50.

front: In Lab 1 Part B, what is the least n with (1/2)^n < 1/1000?
basis: Lab 1 Part B (exact on the grid k/200)

front: In Lab 1 Part C, what value of x^100 at x = 0.99 is printed?
back: 0.3660323413, to ten decimals.

front: When is a subset K of a metric space compact (Definition 1.1)?
back: When every sequence in K has a subsequence that converges to a point of K. This is sequential compactness.

front: In Lemma 1.2 (nested closed intervals). Hypotheses: I_k = [a_k, b_k] for k ≥ 1 with I_1 ⊇ I_2 ⊇ ⋯, and b_k − a_k → 0. What is the point s, and why does it lie in every I_k?
back: s = sup_k a_k, which exists by the supremum property of L01. Each a_k ≤ s, and s ≤ b_k because b_k bounds every a_j.

front: Proposition 1.3 (Bolzano–Weierstrass). Hypotheses: (x_n) is a real sequence, and there are reals a ≤ b with a ≤ x_n ≤ b for all n. What is the conclusion?
back: (x_n) has a subsequence that converges to a real number.

front: Proposition 1.4. Hypotheses: a ≤ b are real, and [a, b] carries the Euclidean distance. What is the conclusion?
back: [a, b] is a compact metric space.

front: Is the open interval (0, 1) compact?
back: No. The sequence 1/(n + 1) in (0, 1) has every subsequence converging to 0, which is not in (0, 1) (Example 1.5).

front: Proposition 2.1. Hypotheses: (X, d) is a metric space; K ⊆ X is nonempty and compact; f: X → R is continuous. What is the conclusion?
back: There are p and q in K with f(q) ≤ f(x) ≤ f(p) for every x in K.

front: Corollary 2.2 (extreme value theorem). Hypotheses: a ≤ b are real, and f: [a, b] → R is continuous. What is the conclusion?
back: f attains a maximum and a minimum on [a, b].

front: Proposition 3.1. Hypotheses: (X, d) is a metric space; (x_n) is Cauchy in X; some subsequence converges to x in X. What is the conclusion?
back: The whole sequence converges to x.

front: Corollary 3.2. Hypotheses: (X, d) is a metric space, and K ⊆ X is compact with the restricted metric. What is the conclusion?
back: Every Cauchy sequence in K converges to a point of K, so K is complete.

front: Proposition 3.4 (unit vectors). Hypotheses: B(N) is the bounded real sequences with d∞; e_n(k) = 1 if k = n and 0 otherwise. What is the conclusion?
back: d∞(e_m, e_n) = 1 for all m ≠ n, so no subsequence converges. The closed unit ball is bounded but not compact.

front: Does every bounded sequence converge?
back: No. (−1)^n is bounded and has no limit. Boundedness gives a convergent subsequence (here the odd terms, which converge to −1), not convergence (Misconception 1).

front: Is a bounded set compact?
back: No. The open interval (0, 1) is bounded and not compact (Example 1.5). The closed unit ball in B(N) is bounded and not compact (Proposition 3.4).

front: Does a continuous function on a bounded set attain its maximum?
back: No. f(x) = x on (0, 1) is continuous and bounded but has no maximum. Corollary 2.2 needs a closed bounded interval, which is compact (Proposition 1.4).

front: In Lab 1 Part A, what index is chosen at step 8?
back: Index 55, in the interval [3/128, 7/256] of width 1/256.
basis: Lab 1 Part A (finite prefix of 4096 terms; illustrates the construction only)

front: In Lab 1 Part B, what is the largest value of x(1 − x) on the grid k/7, and where is it attained?
back: 12/49, at x = 3/7, the first grid point that attains it. That is below the true maximum 1/4, because 1/2 is not on the grid.

front: In Lab 1 Part C, how many pairs of the unit vectors e_0 to e_9 of length 20 are checked, and what distances occur?
back: 45 pairs, all at sup distance 1.

front: What is a contraction mapping with modulus β on a metric space (Definition 1.1)?
back: A map φ: X → X with 0 < β < 1 and d(φx, φy) ≤ β d(x, y) for all x and y, with the same β for every pair.

front: Proposition 1.5. Hypotheses: a ≤ b are real, I = [a, b] carries d(x, y) = |x − y|, and every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges. Is (I, d) a complete metric space?
back: Yes. A Cauchy sequence in [a, b] converges in R to some x, and a ≤ x ≤ b because a ≤ x_n ≤ b for every term.

front: Proposition 1.4. Hypotheses: (X, d) is a metric space; φ: X → X satisfies d(φx, φy) ≤ β d(x, y) for all x and y, with 0 < β < 1. What is the conclusion?
back: φ is continuous at every point of X.

front: Banach fixed-point theorem (Theorem 2.1, conclusion a). Hypotheses: (X, d) is a complete metric space and X is nonempty; φ is a contraction with modulus β, 0 < β < 1; x0 is in X and x_{n+1} = φ x_n. What is the number of fixed points of φ?
back: Exactly one: φ has a unique fixed point x̄.

front: Theorem 2.1(c). Hypotheses: (X, d) is a complete metric space and X is nonempty; φ is a contraction with modulus β, 0 < β < 1; x0 is in X and x_{n+1} = φ x_n. What a priori bound does part (c) give?
back: d(x_n, x̄) ≤ β^n d(x0, x1)/(1 − β) for every n ≥ 0. It uses only x0, x1 and β, so it is known once x1 is computed, before the later iterates.

front: Lemma 2.2 (step estimate). Hypotheses: (X, d) is a complete metric space and X is nonempty; φ is a contraction with modulus β, 0 < β < 1; x0 is in X and x_{n+1} = φ x_n; c = d(x0, x1). What bound does the lemma give on d(x_{k+1}, x_k) for k ≥ 0?
back: d(x_{k+1}, x_k) ≤ β^k c for every k ≥ 0.

front: Where is the proof of Lesson 7, Proposition 2.4 (C_b(S) with the sup metric is complete) given?
back: Lesson 5, Proposition 3.2 with X = S. Lesson 7 does not repeat that proof.
basis: Proof by reference to Lesson 5, Proposition 3.2 (Lesson 7, Proposition 2.4)

front: Assuming Assumption 1, Proposition 3.1 (derivative bound). Hypotheses: I = [a, b] with a < b; f: I → R is continuously differentiable; L = sup over I of |f'| is finite. What is the conclusion?
back: |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ L|x − y| for all x and y in I.

front: Assuming Assumption 1, Corollary 3.2. Hypotheses: I = [a, b] with a < b; f: I → R is continuously differentiable; L = sup over I of |f'| is finite; f(I) ⊆ I; and 0 < L < 1. What is the conclusion?
back: f is a contraction mapping of the complete metric space (I, |·|) with modulus L.

front: For φx = x/3 + 2 on R from x0 = 0, is the a priori bound of Theorem 2.1(c) attained?
back: Yes. The error |x_n − 3| = 3 · 3^(−n) equals the bound (1/3)^n · 2/(2/3) at every n (Example 2.3).

front: For φx = βx on R with 0 < β < 1 and x0 = 1, is the a priori bound of Theorem 2.1(c) attained?
back: Yes. The bound equals the error β^n at every n, since d(x0, x1) = 1 − β (Problem R1).

front: What is the modulus of cos on [0, 1], and why does Corollary 3.2 apply?
back: sin 1 ≈ 0.841471, because sup |f'| = sin 1 on [0, 1], and cos maps [0, 1] into (0, 1].

front: Do contractions carry Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences?
back: Yes. d(φa_n, φa_m) ≤ β d(a_n, a_m) ≤ d(a_n, a_m) for n, m large. The argument uses only the contraction inequality, not completeness (Problem P3).

front: On (0, 1] with d(x, y) = |x − y| and φx = x/2, does φ have a fixed point?
back: No. φ is a contraction of modulus 1/2 with no fixed point in (0, 1], because its only candidate is 0, which is not in (0, 1]. Completeness fails.

front: If d(φx, φy) < d(x, y) for every pair of distinct points, is φ a contraction?
back: A contraction needs one β < 1 that works for all pairs. The map φx = √(x² + 1) on R shrinks every distinct pair, but the ratio tends to 1 for pairs of fixed separation far from the origin (x = y + h, y → ∞), and φ has no fixed point (Misconception 1).

front: Must a contraction be differentiable?
back: No. φx = |x|/2 is a contraction with modulus 1/2 and is not differentiable at 0. Proposition 3.1 is sufficient, not necessary (Misconception 2).

front: Does the bound β^n d(x0, x1)/(1 − β) estimate the error using the current iterate?
back: No. It uses only x0, x1 and β. For cosine at n = 5 in Lab 1, the bound is about 48.9 times the error (Misconception 3).
basis: Lab 1 Part A (cosine iteration, n = 5 row)

front: In Lab 1 Part A, what fixed point x̄ does the cosine iteration reach?
In Lab 1 Part B, what is the largest sampled difference quotient of cos on the 201-point grid of [0, 1], and how does it compare with sin 1?
back: 0.840117, which is below sin 1 = 0.841471.

front: In Lab 1 Part C, what is the largest sampled ratio of f(x) = √(x² + 1) on the 201-point grid of [−50, 50]?
back: 0.999798, which is below 1 (Lab 1 Part C).

front: What is the feasible set F(k) from a state k on the grid G?
back: F(k) = {k' in G : k' ≤ k^α}, the next states that k^α can afford. Choosing k' leaves consumption k^α − k' (Section 1).

front: What is a value function on G (Section 1)?
back: A real function V on G that gives the discounted utility of the best plan from each state.

front: What is the discounted Bellman operator B (Definition 1.1)?
back: (BV)(k) = max over k' in F(k) of {√(k^α − k') + β V(k')}, for k in G. The maximum is over a finite set, so it is attained.

front: What is the contraction property of an operator B with modulus β (Definition 2.1)?
back: ‖BV − BW‖∞ ≤ β‖V − W‖∞ for all V and W in R^G, with 0 < β < 1.

front: Proposition 1.3. Hypotheses: G is a finite set of K ≥ 1 points; d(V, W) = ‖V − W‖∞ on R^G. What is the conclusion?
back: (R^G, d) is a complete metric space.

front: If every F(k) is nonempty, does B map R^G into R^G?
back: Yes. Each maximum is over a finite nonempty set, so it is attained (Remark on well-definedness).

front: Theorem 2.2(a). Hypotheses: G = (g_1, …, g_K) is a finite grid of positive numbers with F(k) nonempty for every k; α is in (0, 1); u(c) = √c for c ≥ 0; 0 < β < 1. What is the conclusion?
back: B has the contraction property with modulus β: ‖BV − BW‖∞ ≤ β‖V − W‖∞.

front: Theorem 2.2(b). Hypotheses: G = (g_1, …, g_K) is a finite grid of positive numbers with F(k) nonempty for every k; α is in (0, 1); u(c) = √c for c ≥ 0; 0 < β < 1. What does B have?
back: Exactly one fixed point V*, so that V*(k) = max over k' in F(k) of {√(k^α − k') + β V*(k')} for each k in G.

front: Theorem 2.2(c). Hypotheses: G = (g_1, …, g_K) is a finite grid of positive numbers with F(k) nonempty for every k; α is in (0, 1); u(c) = √c for c ≥ 0; 0 < β < 1. For every starting function V0, what bound do the iterates V_{n+1} = BV_n satisfy?
back: ‖V_n − V*‖∞ ≤ β^n ‖V_1 − V_0‖∞/(1 − β), and V_n converges to V*.

front: Example 2.3 (one state). Take G = (1/4) and α = 1/2. What is the fixed point of B at β = 0.9?
On the four-point grid with α = 1/2 and β = 1, starting from V0 = 0, what lower bound does V_n(0.25) satisfy?
back: V_n(0.25) ≥ n/2 for every n, so the iterates are unbounded (Problem R2).

front: For β, θ in (0, 1), how far apart are the operators B_β and B_θ on the same grid?
back: For each fixed V, ‖B_β V − B_θ V‖∞ ≤ |β − θ| ‖V‖∞, so BV depends Lipschitz-continuously on β, with constant ‖V‖∞ (Problem R1).

front: Can the maximum over feasible choices break the contraction, because a maximum is not linear?
back: No. The proof compares each maximiser with the other operator's value at the same point and needs no linearity. It uses three facts: each F(k) is finite and nonempty, F(k) is the same set for V and W, and β ≥ 0 (Misconception 1).

front: Does a larger discount factor give a stronger contraction?
back: No. The modulus is β, so a larger β gives a weaker contraction, because the bound β‖V − W‖∞ is larger (Misconception 2).

front: Is the grid fixed point the value of the continuous savings problem?
back: No. V* is an object of the grid model, the fixed point of the grid operator on four states. A finer or continuous state space has a different operator, and the difference is the discretization error (Misconception 3).

front: In Lab 1 Part A, what value V*(0.25) does iteration from zero give?
In Lab 1 Part B, what is the largest sampled contraction ratio over 2000 seeded pairs?
back: The largest sampled ratio is 0.900000, which equals β = 0.9 to six decimal places.

front: In Lab 1 Part A, what is V*(0.5)?
back: V*(0.5) = 5.176097 (Problem E2 checks the value by hand).

front: How does the solver's iteration count change with β on the four-point grid?
back: It rises: 40 iterations at β = 0.5, 257 at β = 0.9 (Lab 1), and 527 at β = 0.95, from copies of the lab with BETA changed.
basis: Problem E1 (copies of the Lab 1 twin with BETA changed)

front: What is value-function iteration from V0 (Definition 2.1)?
back: The sequence V_{n+1} = BV_n for n ≥ 0. V_n is the iterate after n steps.

front: What is the certified error after n steps (Definition 2.2)?
back: cert_n = β/(1 − β) · ‖V_n − V_{n−1}‖∞ for n ≥ 1. It uses two computed iterates and does not use V*.

front: In Lemma 1.1 (G finite, d(V, W) = ‖V − W‖∞), why does a Cauchy sequence of functions in R^G have a limit, and what limit is it?
back: For each k in G the real sequence V_m(k) is Cauchy, so it converges to some a(k) by completeness of R. Since G is finite, the maximum of the finitely many errors |V_m(k) − a(k)| tends to zero, so V_m → a in the sup norm.

front: In Lesson 9, Lemma 1.2 gives a contraction bound for B. What are its hypotheses and conclusion?
back: Hypotheses: 0 < β < 1 and V, W in R^G. Conclusion: ‖BV − BW‖∞ ≤ β‖V − W‖∞.

front: Lemma 2.3(a), under 0 < β < 1 and V_{n+1} = BV_n. For n ≥ 1, what bound does the iteration give for the step ‖V_{n+1} − V_n‖∞?
back: ‖V_{n+1} − V_n‖∞ ≤ β‖V_n − V_{n−1}‖∞, by Lemma 1.2 applied to V_n and V_{n−1}.

front: Lemma 2.3(b), under 0 < β < 1, V_{n+1} = BV_n and V* the fixed point of Theorem 1.3. For n ≥ 0, what inequality links the distance to V* and the next step?
Lemma 2.3(c). Hypotheses: 0 < β < 1; V_{n+1} = BV_n; V* is the fixed point of Theorem 1.3. For n ≥ 1, what does the certified error bound?
back: ‖V_n − V*‖∞ ≤ β/(1 − β) · ‖V_n − V_{n−1}‖∞, so cert_n bounds the error.

front: Theorem 2.4 (certified stopping rule). Hypotheses: 0 < β < 1; V_{n+1} = BV_n; a tolerance τ > 0; N is the first n ≥ 1 with cert_n ≤ τ. What is the conclusion?
back: N is finite, and ‖V_N − V*‖∞ ≤ cert_N ≤ τ.

front: Does Ψ(x) = x + 1 on R have a fixed point, and what happens to β/(1 − β) at β = 1?
back: No fixed point exists, since |Ψ(x) − x| = 1 everywhere. The factor β/(1 − β) is undefined at β = 1 (Section 3, item 2).

front: On R with Ψ(x) = βx + 1 and V0 = 0, how does |V1 − ξ*| compare with β/(1 − β)|V1 − V0|?
back: They are equal for every β in (0, 1), because V1 = 1 and ξ* = 1/(1 − β). So no smaller constant works for this family at n = 1 (Section 3, item 3).
basis: Section 3 (canon breaks, item 3) and Problem R3

front: What is β/(1 − β) for β = 0.5, 0.9 and 0.99?
On the four-point grid of Lesson 9, with β = 0.9, what is the smallest n for which the a priori bound (β^n/(1 − β))‖V1 − V0‖∞ is at most 10^(−6)?
back: n = 152. With ‖V1 − V0‖∞ = √3/2, the bound is 1.067 × 10^(−6) at n = 151 and 9.60 × 10^(−7) at n = 152. The certified stop needs only 147 steps.
basis: Problem R2 (arithmetic shown in the solution)

front: In Lab 1, how many iterations does the reference solve take?
back: 278 iterations.

front: In Lab 1, how many iterations does each certified stop take at tolerances 10^(−2), 10^(−4) and 10^(−6)?
back: 59, 103 and 147 iterations.

front: In Lab 1, after how many steps does the naive rule stop when the last step is at most 10^(−6)?
back: 126 steps.

front: In Lab 1, what is the certified error after a fixed count of 10 steps?
back: 1.7433922005, which equals the actual error. The certificate is valid, but it is far above 10^(−6).

front: Is a small step between two iterates a bound on the error?
back: Not by itself. Lemma 2.3(c) bounds the error by β/(1 − β) times the step, which is nine times the step at β = 0.9 (Misconception 1).

front: Does the certificate of Theorem 2.4 bound the error against the continuous savings problem?
back: No. cert_N bounds ‖V_N − V*‖∞, the distance to the fixed point of the grid operator on G, and the discretization error is not covered (Misconception 2, Remark 2.5).

front: Does a fixed number of iterations give a certified answer?
back: Not by itself. A certificate is cert_N compared with a tolerance τ (Theorem 2.4), and a fixed count has no tolerance attached until its certificate is compared with one (Misconception 3).

front: What is a tagged partition of [a, b] (Section 1)?
back: A partition a = x_0 < x_1 < ⋯ < x_n = b with a tag ξ_i in I_i = [x_{i−1}, x_i] for each i.

front: What is the Riemann–Stieltjes sum S(P, ξ) (Definition 1.1)?
back: The sum over the subintervals of f(ξ_i)(G(x_i) − G(x_{i−1})).

front: When does the Riemann–Stieltjes integral of f with respect to G equal I (Definition 1.2)?
back: When for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that |S(P, ξ) − I| < ε for every tagged partition with mesh below δ. Partitions are not refined, and the tags are arbitrary.

front: Lemma 1.3. Hypotheses: f and G are real functions on [a, b] with a < b; I and I' both satisfy Definition 1.2 for f and G. What is the conclusion?
back: I = I'. When the integral exists, it is unique.

front: Lemma 2.1. Hypotheses: a < b, and f is continuous on [a, b]. What is the conclusion?
back: f is bounded on [a, b], and for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with |f(s) − f(t)| < ε whenever |s − t| < δ.

front: Lemma 2.2. Hypotheses: a < b, and h is continuous on [a, b]. What is the conclusion?
back: h is integrable on [a, b] in the Darboux sense of M2 Lesson 9.

front: Assuming Assumption 1, Theorem 3.1. Hypotheses: a < b; f is continuous on [a, b]; G is continuously differentiable on [a, b]. What is the conclusion?
back: Assuming Assumption 1, the integral ∫_a^b f dG exists and equals ∫_a^b f(x)G'(x) dx.
basis: Proof in Section 3 (Theorem 3.1; uses Lemmas 2.1, 2.2, 2.4, (Q2) and Assumption 1 (Q3))

front: Assuming Assumption 1, Corollary 3.2. Hypotheses: f(x) = x and G(x) = x² on [0, 1]. What is ∫_0^1 x d(x²)?
back: Assuming Assumption 1, 2/3, because Theorem 3.1 gives 2 ∫_0^1 x² dx and ∫_0^1 x² dx = 1/3.

front: For f = x and G = x² on a uniform partition into n parts, what is the right-tag sum?
basis: Example 3.3 (proved on the page); Lab 1 Part A checks it

front: Assuming Assumption 1, for f = x and G = x² on [0, 1], what bound on |S − 2/3| follows from the proof of Theorem 3.1, in terms of the mesh m?
back: Assuming Assumption 1, |S − 2/3| ≤ 2m, since sup |G'| = 2 and η is replaced by the mesh m (Example 3.3).
basis: Example 3.3 (the proof of Theorem 3.1 with η replaced by the mesh)

front: Assuming Assumption 1, for f = x and G = x² on [0, 1], what sharper bound does Problem P2 establish for a tagged partition of mesh m?
back: Assuming Assumption 1, |S − 2/3| ≤ m.

front: Proposition 4.1. Hypotheses: f = 1 on [1/2, 1] and f = 0 on [0, 1/2); G is the step integrator with G = 0 below 1/2 and G = 1 from 1/2 on. What is the conclusion?
back: No real number I satisfies Definition 1.2 for f and G.

front: Proposition 4.2. Hypotheses: f(x) = x on [0, 1]; G is the step integrator at 1/2. What is the conclusion?
back: For every tagged partition, |S(P, ξ) − 1/2| ≤ |P|, so ∫_0^1 f dG = 1/2.

front: Does monotonicity of G rescue the integral when f is discontinuous at the jump?
back: No. For f(x) = 0 below 1/2 and f(x) = 1 from 1/2 on [0, 1], Proposition 4.1 gives no Riemann–Stieltjes integral against the step integrator G at 1/2, even though G is nondecreasing (Remark 4.2).

front: For f continuous on [0, 1], c in (0, 1), and G the step at c, what is ∫_0^1 f dG?
back: f(c). Problem R2 proves it by the argument of Proposition 4.2.

front: Assuming Assumption 1, what is ∫_0^1 x d(x³)?
back: 3/4, because Theorem 3.1 (under Assumption 1) gives ∫_0^1 x · 3x² dx = 3 ∫_0^1 x³ dx = 3/4.

front: For f continuous and G(x) = x on [a, b], does ∫ f dG equal the ordinary integral?
back: Yes, under Assumption 1. G' = 1 is continuous, so Theorem 3.1 gives ∫_a^b f dG = ∫_a^b f(x) dx (Problem P3).

front: When G is increasing, does ∫ f dG equal ∫ f dx?
back: No. ∫_0^1 x d(x²) = 2/3 (Corollary 3.2, under Assumption 1), while ∫_0^1 x dx = 1/2. The integrator enters the sums (Misconception 1).

front: Is a discontinuous integrand harmless when the mesh is small?
back: No. Against the step integrator, the tagged sums are 0 and 1 on partitions of meshes 0.1 and 0.01 (Lab 1 Part C). Shrinking the mesh does not remove the jump (Misconception 2).
basis: Lab 1 Part C (step integrator, meshes 0.1 and 0.01)

front: Does ∫ f dG = ∫ f G' dx hold for every nondecreasing G?
back: No. Theorem 3.1 requires G to be continuously differentiable. The step integrator is nondecreasing but has no derivative at 1/2, and ∫_0^1 x dG = 1/2 for it (Misconception 3).

front: In Lab 1 Part A, what right-tag sum does n = 1000 give, and what is its error from 2/3?
In Lab 1 Part B, what is the largest ratio of error to mesh over the 200 seeded tagged partitions?
back: 0.491631 in this sample, so every error is below half of its partition's mesh.

front: In Lab 1 Part D, what right-tag and left-tag sums does the identity integrator G(x) = x give at n = 1000?
back: 0.500500000000 and 0.499500000000, each within 0.0005 of 1/2, one above it and one below it.

front: On one grid point with utility u and 0 < β < 1, starting from V0 = 0 and V_{n+1} = u + βV_n, what is the error |V_n − V*|?
back: u β^n/(1 − β), where V* = u/(1 − β). The bound of Theorem 2.2(c) holds with equality (Problem P3).

front: For h and g integrable on [c, d] with c < d (and M ≥ 0 for the estimate), what three properties does Lemma 2.4 give for the integral?
back: Monotonicity: if h ≤ g on [c, d], then the integral of h is at most the integral of g. Estimate: if |h| ≤ M, then |integral of h| ≤ M(d − c). Additivity: for c < e < d, the integral over [c, d] is the sum of the integrals over [c, e] and [e, d].

front: What is the total variation V(G) of G on [a, b] (Definition 3.4)?
back: The supremum, over all partitions P of [a, b], of the sum of |G(x_i) − G(x_{i−1})|.

front: Theorem 3.5 (continuous integrand, bounded-variation integrator). Hypotheses: a < b; f is continuous on [a, b]; G has bounded variation on [a, b]. What is the conclusion?
back: The Riemann–Stieltjes integral of f with respect to G on [a, b] exists, so some real I satisfies Definition 1.2. This is existence only; the value is not given as the integral of f G'.

front: What is the sup distance d∞(f, g) between bounded real functions f and g on a nonempty set S (Example 1.6)?
back: d∞(f, g) = sup over x in S of |f(x) − g(x)|. It is a real number when f and g are bounded (Proposition 1.7), and on a finite S it is a maximum.

front: What is a maximum of a set A of real numbers (Section 1)?
back: An element of A that is also an upper bound of A.

front: Is d(x, y) = |x² − y²| on R a metric?
back: No. It satisfies M2 and M3, but d(1, −1) = 0 with 1 ≠ −1, so M1 fails and d is a pseudometric (Problem set, Proof 1).

front: When is a set of real numbers bounded, and when is a function bounded (Section 1)?
back: A set of real numbers is bounded when some real M ≥ 0 satisfies |v| ≤ M for every member v. A function is bounded when the set of its values is bounded.

front: What is a subsequence of (x_n) (Section 1)?
back: A sequence (x_{n_k}) with n_1 < n_2 < ⋯, taken from the terms of (x_n) in their order.

front: What is a fixed point of a map φ: X → X (Section 1)?
back: A point x̄ with φ x̄ = x̄.

front: What is a Lipschitz bound with constant L on an interval I (Section 3)?
back: An inequality |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ L|x − y| for all x and y in I, with one constant L for every pair of points.

front: Can the modulus sin 1 of cos on [0, 1] be lowered (Problem R3)?
back: No. Taking y = 1 and x = 1 − h, the quotient |cos x − cos 1|/|x − 1| tends to sin 1 as h → 0, so no β′ < sin 1 works for all x, y in [0, 1].

front: What is a policy for the grid model (Section 1)?
back: A rule that gives a next state k′ in F(k) for each state k.

front: What is the sup norm on R^G (Section 1)?
back: ‖V‖∞ = max over k in G of |V(k)|. The distance between V and W is ‖V − W‖∞.

front: When is a metric space (X, d) complete (Definition 3.2)?
back: When every Cauchy sequence in X converges to a point of X.

front: Theorem 1.3 (Banach, on R^G) needs (X, d) complete and nonempty, and a contraction of modulus β in (0, 1). Applied to B on R^G, which two lemmas of Lesson 9 supply the completeness and the contraction?
back: Lemma 1.1 (R^G with the sup norm is complete) and Lemma 1.2 (B is a contraction with modulus β in (0, 1)). Theorem 1.3 then gives exactly one fixed point V* and V_n → V* from every V_0.

front: In Lab 1 Part C, what is the minimum of f(x) − x on the 201-point grid of [−50, 50], for f(x) = √(x² + 1)?
back: 0.009999. It is positive at every grid point, but the grid does not establish that f has no fixed point; Section 4 establishes that. (Lab 1 Part C)

front: In Lab 1 Part A, what residual does the printed fixed point give?
back: 8.695e-13, below the stated 1e-9.

front: In Lab 1 Part C, what does the one-point grid give after 1000 iterations at β = 1?
back: V = 500.000000, which is n/2 for n = 1000 (Lab 1 Part C, float).

front: In Lab 1, how do the actual and certified errors compare at each certified stop?
back: They are equal to ten decimals.

front: In Lab 1, what actual error does the naive rule leave at its stop, and how does it compare with the last step?
back: 0.0000085808, which is above 10^(−6) and nine times the unrounded last step.

front: In Lab 1 Part B, do all 200 seeded tagged partitions satisfy |S − 2/3| ≤ 2 · mesh?
back: Yes. All 200 satisfy the bound, and the lab's flag all_within_2_mesh prints True.

front: Banach fixed-point theorem (Theorem 2.1, conclusion b). Hypotheses: (X, d) is a complete metric space and X is nonempty; φ is a contraction with modulus β, 0 < β < 1; x0 is in X and x_{n+1} = φ x_n. What does the sequence (x_n) do?
back: x_n → x̄ for every starting point x0, where x̄ is the fixed point of φ.

front: Lemma 2.2 (distance between iterates). Hypotheses: (X, d) is a complete metric space and X is nonempty; φ is a contraction with modulus β, 0 < β < 1; x0 is in X and x_{n+1} = φ x_n; c = d(x0, x1). What bound does the lemma give on d(x_n, x_m) for m > n ≥ 0?
back: d(x_n, x_m) ≤ β^n c/(1 − β).

front: On the grid G = (2, 3) with α = 1/2, what is F(2), and why is the Bellman operator undefined there?
back: F(2) is empty: the output √2 ≈ 1.414 lies below both grid points, so the maximum in Definition 1.1 is over an empty set.

front: When is a sequence (s_n) of real numbers bounded (Section 2)?
back: When some real number C satisfies |s_n| ≤ C for every n.

front: When is a set of real numbers bounded below (Section 2)?
back: When some real number m satisfies m ≤ b for every member b of the set. Such an m is a lower bound of the set.

front: When is a subset K of a metric space X closed (Section 2)?
back: When its complement X ∖ K is open.

front: Does Definition 1.1 (completeness) say anything about the set N of natural numbers?
back: No. N is nonempty but has no upper bound (Theorem 1.2), so the bounded-above hypothesis of Definition 1.1 fails for N.

front: In Lab 1, what is the smallest gap S_2N − S_N over N = 1 to 200, and at which N does it occur?
basis: Lab 1 (finite range N = 1 to 200; Proposition 3.3 covers all N)

front: In Lab 1, do all grid points within δ = 1/50 of 2 satisfy |x² − 4| < 1/10?
back: Yes, all seven satisfy it.

front: In Lab 1 with δ = 1/10, which is the first grid point with |x − 2| < 1/10 and |x² − 4| ≥ 1/10?
In Lab 1 Part A, how many triangle-inequality failures are printed?
basis: Lab 1 Part A (finite sample; Proposition 1.4 covers all points)

front: In Lab 1 Part A, how does the value of x^n at x = 1/2 change as the order n grows from 1 to 50?
back: It shrinks from 1/2 (order 1) to 1/2^50 (order 50).
basis: Lab 1 Part A (the value at x = 1/2 column)

front: In Lab 1 Part B, does the sup distance equal (1/2)^n for each printed order?
back: Yes, equals_half_power is True for orders 1, 2, 5, 10 and 50.
basis: Lab 1 Part B (exact on the grid k/200)

back: Yes, tail_values_in_their_interval is True.
basis: Lab 1 Part A (finite prefix of 4096 terms; illustrates the construction only)

front: In Lab 1 Part A, does the error stay at most the a priori bound for n = 0 to 30?
back: Yes, at every n from 0 to 30.

front: Lesson 7, Definition 1.2 uses the completeness of R with d(x, y) = |x − y|. Which result gives it?
back: Lesson 2, Theorem 2.5: every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges, proved from the completeness axiom (Lesson 1, Definition 1.1).

front: For the one-state operator of Example 2.3, is |BV − BW| = β|V − W| exactly, so that the modulus β is attained?
back: Yes.

front: In Lab 1 Part A, how many iterations does iteration from zero take to reach a successive gap of at most 1e-12?
back: 257 iterations.

front: In Lab 1 Part B, does any sampled ratio exceed β by more than 10^(−12)?
back: No. The lab's check passes at tolerance 10^(−12).

In Lab 1, what certified error does the reference solve reach?
In Lab 1, which next capital does the reference policy choose at every grid point?
back: 0.25 at every grid point.

front: In Lab 1, does each certified error stay at most its tolerance?
back: Yes, cert_within_tol is True at 10^(−2), 10^(−4) and 10^(−6).

front: For f = x and G = x² on a uniform partition into n parts, what is the left-tag sum?
basis: Example 3.3 (proved on the page); Lab 1 Part A checks it

front: For f = x and G = x² on a uniform partition into n parts, do the right-tag and left-tag sums both differ from 2/3 by at most 1/n?
back: Yes (Example 3.3).
basis: Example 3.3 (proved on the page); Lab 1 Part A checks it

front: Which result of Lesson 8 does Lemma 1.2 of Lesson 9 restate?
back: Part (a) of Theorem 2.2 of Lesson 8. Lesson 9 repeats its proof in Section 1.

front: What is the mesh of a partition P of [a, b] (Section 1)?
back: The largest subinterval length, max Δx_i, where Δx_i = x_i − x_{i−1}.

front: When does G have bounded variation on [a, b] (Definition 3.4)?
back: When V(G) is finite.

front: If G is nondecreasing on [a, b], what is V(G) (Definition 3.4)?

front: When is G continuously differentiable on [a, b] (Section 3)?
back: When G has a derivative at every point of [a, b] (one-sided at a and b), and G′ is continuous on [a, b].

front: When is a subset A of a metric space (X, d) bounded (Section 1)?
back: When some x0 in X and some R ≥ 0 satisfy d(x0, x) ≤ R for every x in A.

front: Lesson 7, Proposition 2.4. Hypotheses: S is a metric space; C_b(S) is the set of bounded continuous real functions on S; d∞(f, g) = sup over s in S of |f(s) − g(s)|, which is finite for f, g in C_b(S); every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges. What is the conclusion?
back: (C_b(S), d∞) is a complete metric space.
